title: Ladder Inspection and Removal From Service

content.overview: A ladder that was safe yesterday can be unsafe today after impact, contamination, wear, missing hardware, or unauthorized modification. OSHA's ladder requirements include inspection before initial use in each work shift and as necessary to identify defects. A pre-use inspection is therefore a decision process: identify conditions that could affect safe use, compare them with the equipment's intended condition, and remove defective equipment from service instead of passing the risk to the next worker.

vocabulary.definition: A deliberate check performed before equipment is used to identify visible damage, missing parts, contamination, or other unsafe conditions.
Damage, deterioration, missing components, deformation, contamination, or another condition that can make equipment unsafe for intended use.
A controlled action that prevents defective equipment from being used until it is repaired as permitted or replaced.

sections.title: Inspect systematically
sections.body: Use the same sequence each time so obvious and subtle defects are less likely to be skipped. Check side rails, steps or rungs, feet, spreaders or locking components, fasteners, labels needed for correct use, and visible contamination that could affect footing or grip. Look for bending, cracking, corrosion, missing parts, loose hardware, damaged anti-slip components, or repairs and modifications that are not part of the approved equipment condition. The inspection should also confirm the ladder is the right type and capacity for the planned use.

sections.title: Defective means unavailable
sections.body: OSHA requires ladders with structural or other defects to be immediately tagged 'Dangerous: Do Not Use' or with similar language and removed from service until repaired or replaced. A worker should not leave a questionable ladder in the normal storage location with a verbal warning only. The control must make the equipment unavailable to another user who did not hear the conversation.

sections.title: Document recurring conditions
sections.body: A single damaged ladder needs removal; repeated ladder damage needs investigation. If feet are repeatedly contaminated, rails are being struck in storage, or labels are disappearing, the workplace should correct the storage, cleaning, traffic, or purchasing system that produces the defect. Record the equipment identity, defect, action taken, and escalation when the local safety system requires it. The goal is both immediate risk control and prevention of recurrence.

workedExamples: A step ladder has a loose spreader and one damaged foot. Tag it out and remove it from service; do not use a coworker to hold it steady as a substitute for safe condition.

A ladder is structurally intact but has wet nutrient residue on two steps. Clean and dry it using the facility procedure, then recheck the surface before use rather than assuming contamination is harmless.
commonMistakes: Inspecting only the steps while ignoring rails, feet, locks, fasteners, and contamination.
Leaving defective equipment in normal storage with an informal warning.
Treating repeated damage as isolated bad luck instead of investigating storage and handling causes.
content.practicalApplication: Perform a documented inspection on an actual or simulated ladder. Identify at least six inspection points, classify each as acceptable or requiring action, and demonstrate how a defective ladder would be tagged and physically removed from normal availability.
content.summary: A ladder inspection is only effective when defects lead to controlled action. Use a repeatable inspection sequence, remove defective equipment from service, and investigate recurring damage patterns so hazards are not transferred between workers.
